query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing spark plasma sintering (SPS) by using ultrafast heating rates combined with high uniaxial pressures and a very short dwell time at temperatures around or below 1700 °C will enable the formation of a fully bonded, refined single‐phase ZrB2 microstructure that retains strong Zr–B and B–B interactions while resisting high-temperature oxidation and liquid metal corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase ZrB2 that, when conventionally processed at very high temperatures (>2300 °C), develops a robust bonding network but is challenging to manufacture at lower temperatures. Lower-temperature processing (<1700 °C) in earlier studies results in materials with incomplete bonding networks and vulnerabilities to oxidation and liquid plating-metal corrosion.
generation.intervention: Apply an optimized SPS route with ultrafast heating rates, high uniaxial pressure, and minimal dwell time at ≤1700 °C to produce a near fully densified, refined ZrB2 microstructure.
generation.conditions: Sintering performed in an inert or vacuum atmosphere, with peak temperatures maintained at or below 1700 °C, rapid heating (on the order of seconds per degree), high applied pressure during sintering, and a very short dwell time to prevent grain coarsening.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, fully dense microstructure with limited porosity and optimized grain boundaries that reinforce the Zr–B and B–B bonding network while minimizing oxidation pathways.
generation.mechanism: The ultrafast heating and high pressure promote rapid densification and immediate formation of strong interatomic bonds, achieving a well-developed, single-phase ZrB2 even at temperatures much lower than traditional processing. The refined grain boundaries and reduced porosity act as barriers to oxygen ingress and corrosive species from liquid plating metals.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with conventionally sintered ZrB2 (>2300 °C) and earlier low-temperature specimens, the SPS-processed ZrB2 is expected to exhibit comparable mechanical strength and structural integrity with significantly improved resistance to high-temperature oxidation and liquid metal corrosion.
generation.baseline: Single-phase ZrB2 prepared by high-temperature (>2300 °C) methods (with excellent bonding but challenging to produce) and lower-temperature (<1700 °C) specimens from earlier studies which lacked sufficient oxidation and corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: The process is applicable as long as sintering remains at or below 1700 °C and the post-sintering service environment involves high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., up to ~1500 °C) and exposure to liquid plating-metal environments typical of industrial applications.
generation.uncertainty: Although optimized SPS parameters have proven successful in other refractory systems, the precise replication of the full bonding network and long-term stability against oxidation and corrosion in ZrB2 under extended service conditions remains to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of ZrB2 samples: one using the optimized SPS method (ultrafast heating, high uniaxial pressure, short dwell at ≤1700 °C) and a control set using a conventional lower-temperature sintering method. Subject both sets to simulated high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., exposure to air at 1400–1500 °C for extended durations) and liquid plating-metal corrosion tests (immersion in representative molten metal baths).
measurements: Microstructural analysis (SEM, TEM) to evaluate densification and grain boundary integrity.
Mechanical testing (hardness, compressive strength) to assess structural integrity.
Oxidation tests (weight gain, oxide scale thickness, adhesion quality) after high-temperature exposure.
Corrosion tests (mass loss, surface degradation, chemical analysis of corrosion products) following exposure to liquid metal environments.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPS-processed ZrB2 does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in oxidation resistance, liquid metal corrosion resistance, and mechanical properties relative to both the high-temperature processed baseline and the conventional lower-temperature specimens, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. frame.system: Single‐phase ZrB2 ceramic that normally requires very high synthesis temperatures (>2300 °C) to develop its strong Zr–B and B–B bonding network, but in its pure form is prone to oxidation and liquid plating-metal corrosion when processed at lower temperatures.
frame.goal: To enable lower‐temperature manufacturing (≤1700 °C) while delivering a material that meets application requirements in terms of mechanical strength, structural integrity, high-temperature oxidation durability, and resistance to liquid metal corrosion.
frame.limitation: Pure single‐phase ZrB2 either demands excessively high processing temperatures or, when prepared at lower temperatures by previous methods, results in a material that lacks sufficient oxidation resistance and stability in corrosive liquid plating-metal environments.

decision.trend: In the past decade, researchers trying to lower the processing temperature for refractory systems (including high‐entropy and refractory alloy coatings) have increasingly turned to advanced processing routes (e.g., spark plasma sintering, laser cladding) to achieve near‐full densification and refined microstructures at temperatures near 1700 °C. These studies show that while a denser, finer grain structure can improve mechanical strength and offer some resistance to oxidation, they still fall short in delivering robust oxidation protection and resistance to liquid plating-metal corrosion. In other words, the strong intrinsic bonding network of refractory compounds (akin to that in single‐phase ZrB2) is not fully developed when processed below the traditional >2300 °C range, leaving the final body vulnerable to environmental degradation.
decision.unsolved: Despite processing innovations that lower the manufacturing temperature, it remains unresolved how to simultaneously achieve the fully developed bonding network in single-phase ZrB2 and the desirable surface stability needed for high‐temperature oxidation and liquid metal corrosion resistance.
decision.lever: Optimized spark plasma sintering (SPS) using ultrafast heating rates combined with high uniaxial pressures and a very short dwell time at ≤1700 °C
decision.why: Advanced SPS has already proven effective in processing refractory materials near 1700 °C (as seen in related high-density refractory composites) by promoting rapid densification and preventing excessive grain growth. This approach is expected to enable the formation of a well‐developed, fully bonded ZrB2 microstructure that retains the strong Zr–B and B–B interactions, while the refined grain boundaries and limited porosity provide barriers to high-temperature oxidation and liquid plating-metal corrosion. This single intervention directly addresses the root challenge of reproducing the desirable properties of high-temperature, fully sintered ZrB2 using a lower-temperature synthesis route.
